definition.text: Marginalism is the economic theory that explains differences in the value of goods and services by their marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit.

facts.text: It explains why diamonds cost more than water: water has greater total utility, but a diamond has greater marginal utility.
The law of diminishing marginal utility, also called Gossen's First Law, says each added unit of a good brings less extra benefit than the one before, all else equal.
Marginalism explains prices through supply and demand: buyers want less and sellers offer more as the price rises.
Following Alfred Marshall, marginalists also used marginal physical productivity to explain costs.
At the most general level a marginal cost is a marginal opportunity cost, though it usually means the extra money spent.
Marginalism is an integral part of mainstream economic theory.

definition.text: The Marginal Revolution was the shift in the 1870s, led by Jevons, Menger and Walras, to explaining value by marginal utility instead of labour.

facts.text: Jevons proposed the theory in an article in 1862 and a book in 1871; Menger presented it in 1871; Walras published the first part of his work in 1874.
The classical school had held that the labour time needed to produce a good set its value; marginal utility instead focused on the value the consumer got from the good.
Each person was taken to keep consuming until the marginal utility of a good equalled its price.
A second generation, including Alfred Marshall, Böhm-Bawerk, Wieser and Pareto, carried the ideas into the mainstream; Marshall's Principles of Economics appeared in 1890.
Earlier, Daniel Bernoulli's 1738 paper gave the first clear published statement of marginal utility, written to solve a gambling puzzle.
The revolution is often read as a response to the rise of the workers' movement and Marxian economics.

title: Marxist criticism of marginalism

definition.text: Marxist economists rejected marginalism, holding to the labour theory of value and arguing that prices cannot be explained by individual preferences alone.

facts.text: Ernest Mandel argued marginalism ignored production and explained at best short-term price swings, not stable long-run prices.
Maurice Dobb argued marginalist prices depend on the distribution of income, since people's ability to express preferences depends on their spending power.
Some economists in the Marxian tradition, such as Oskar Lange and Michał Kalecki, tried to combine it with marginalism and neoclassical economics.

contested_note: Marxist and mainstream economists disagree over whether marginal utility or labour explains value and prices.

definition.text: A Marshallian demand function gives how much of a good a consumer buys as a function of its price, the consumer's income and the prices of other goods.

facts.text: It solves the utility maximization problem: how a consumer gets the most utility from a given income at given prices.
It is also called uncompensated demand, because a price rise is not offset by extra income, unlike the Hicksian demand function; the response mixes a substitution effect and a wealth effect.
If all prices and income rise by the same factor, the quantities bought stay the same.
With strictly convex preferences and positive prices there is a single best bundle, so demand is unique and continuous.
